content: Loratadine is a medication prescribed to provide temporary relief from symptoms associated with hay fever, such as sneezing, a runny nose, and itching in the eyes, nose, or throat. It is also used to alleviate itching and redness caused by hives. However, it does not prevent hives or other allergic skin reactions. Loratadine belongs to a class of drugs known as antihistamines, which work by blocking histamine, a substance in the body responsible for allergic symptoms. Loratadine is available as a standalone medication or in combination with pseudoephedrine. This information pertains only to loratadine alone; if you are using a combination product, consult the package label or your healthcare provider for additional details. Loratadine is available in various forms, including syrup, tablets, and rapidly disintegrating tablets, all of which are taken orally. It is typically taken once daily, with or without food. Follow the instructions on the package label or those provided by your doctor. Do not exceed the recommended dose, as taking more than directed may cause drowsiness. If using the rapidly disintegrating tablet, carefully remove it from the blister packaging without breaking it, place it on your tongue, and allow it to dissolve. It can be swallowed with or without water. Loratadine should not be used to treat hives that are bruised, blistered, discolored, or non-itchy. If you experience such symptoms, consult your doctor. If your hives do not improve within three days of starting treatment or persist for more than six weeks, stop taking loratadine and contact your doctor. In cases where hives are accompanied by symptoms such as difficulty swallowing, speaking, or breathing; swelling of the mouth, tongue, or surrounding areas; wheezing; drooling; dizziness; or loss of consciousness, seek emergency medical attention immediately. These symptoms may indicate anaphylaxis, a life-threatening allergic reaction. If your doctor suspects you are at risk for anaphylaxis, they may prescribe an epinephrine injector. Loratadine should not be used as a substitute for an epinephrine injector. Before taking loratadine, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to loratadine, any other medications, or any of the ingredients in the product. Review the package label for a list of ingredients. Provide your healthcare provider with a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you are currently taking or plan to take, especially medications for colds and allergies. Notify your doctor if you have a history of asthma, kidney disease, or liver disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking loratadine, contact your healthcare provider. Additionally, if you have phenylketonuria (PKU), be aware that some brands of orally disintegrating tablets may contain phenylalanine. Unless otherwise directed by your doctor, you may continue your normal diet while taking loratadine. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is close to the time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to compensate for a missed one. Loratadine may cause side effects. Common, less severe side effects include headache, dry mouth, nosebleeds, sore throat, mouth sores, difficulty sleeping, nervousness, weakness, stomach pain, diarrhea, and red or itchy eyes. If these symptoms persist or worsen, inform your doctor. Serious side effects include rash, hives, itching, swelling of the face, eyes, lips, tongue, throat, hands, or lower extremities, hoarseness, difficulty breathing or swallowing, and wheezing. If you experience any of these severe side effects, stop taking loratadine and seek immediate medical attention. Store loratadine in its original container, tightly sealed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excessive heat, moisture, and light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Use orally disintegrating tablets immediately after removing them from the blister package and within six months of opening the outer foil pouch. Write the date of opening on the product label to track this timeline. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for guidance on disposal. In the event of an overdose, contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call 911. Symptoms of overdose may include a rapid or pounding heartbeat, drowsiness, headache, or unusual body movements. Keep all scheduled appointments with your doctor while taking loratadine. If you have any questions about the medication, consult your pharmacist. Loratadine is sold under various brand names, including Alavert® Non-Drowsy Allergy Relief 24 Hour, Children's Claritin® Fruit Flavored Syrup 24 Hour, Claritin® 24 Hour, Claritin® Hives Relief, and Claritin® RediTabs® 24 Hour. Combination products containing loratadine and pseudoephedrine include Alavert® Allergy & Sinus D-12 Hour, Claritin-D® 12 Hour, and Claritin-D® 24 Hour.
